extracted.intended_audience: researchers, funding-agency staff, policymakers, and scholars of peer review and research evaluation
extracted.subtask_description: A systematic review synthesizing empirical, inductive studies of the criteria peers use to assess grant applications, producing a taxonomy of evaluated entities and evaluation criteria and mapping criteria-to-entity relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of how novel or innovative the proposed project/aims/outcomes are. Identified as a key evaluation criterion used to judge the aims and outcomes of a proposed project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the single criterion that appeared in all included studies. In the authors' synthesis, originality is used exclusively to assess the project (not applicant or environment). It is part of the cluster of criteria applied to aims/outcomes alongside academic and extra-academic relevance. Considered a core dimension of merit but may be instantiated differently across disciplines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Academic relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the project's significance or relevance to academic audiences, scholarly debates, or contribution to the discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess project aims and outcomes. Appears frequently (present in 8 of the included studies). Distinct from extra-academic relevance; may be operationalized at different levels of abstraction in different studies. Often paired with originality and rigor in assessing intellectual contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-academic relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of the proposed project's relevance or potential impact outside academia (e.g., societal, economic, policy relevance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the most frequent criteria (14% of assigned codes). Used to assess project aims/outcomes and appears in multiple studies (present in 8 studies). Explicitly flagged in the review as a distinct relevance dimension; inclusion of such criteria can introduce non-scientific considerations and contribute to fairness/bias concerns if not clearly defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: A general, higher-level appraisal of the excellence or overall merit of the proposal or components thereof (defined in some studies in broad terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined at a more general level in some studies. Used to evaluate both project and applicant entities. Because 'quality' is multidimensional and variably operationalized, the authors note it occurs less often in a strictly defined form: when used it tends to aggregate several lower-level criteria (e.g., rigor, originality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment whether methods, design, budget, or other features are suitable and fit-for-purpose for the proposed aims and context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frequently used and versatile: appropriateness was one of only three criteria used to assess all three main entities (applicant, project, environment). The review gives examples such as 'appropriateness of the research design' or 'budget–appropriate'. In coding, appropriateness co-occurred with many sub-entities (up to 19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of methodological soundness, robustness, and scientific rigor of the proposed research process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate the proposed research process/content of the project. Appears as part of the set (quality, appropriateness, rigor, coherence/justification) used to judge the research process. Rigor is conceptually distinct from appropriateness and completeness: it concerns methodological thoroughness and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coherence/justification
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the internal logic, argumentation, and justification of the proposal (how well aims, methods, and rationale fit together).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate the proposed research process and project-level reasoning. Often considered together with rigor and appropriateness; includes whether the proposal provides sufficient justification for choices. Can be operationalized as checking for coherent linkage between goals, approach, and expected outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of how clearly the proposal (or parts such as aims, methods, budget) is written and presented (readability, unambiguity, explicitness).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the most frequent criteria (appeared in 10 studies). Treated as a dimension at the level of description (how well the process is described). In coding, clarity applied both to project and applicant entities. Lack of clarity is a common deficiency cited in empirical studies of applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether necessary information, sections, and documentation (e.g., budget details, methods, CV items) are present and sufficiently detailed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears frequently (13% of assigned criteria codes). Considered a description-level criterion (completeness of description). The authors split compound items like 'budget and equipment are described and appropriate' into separate completeness and appropriateness codes. Completeness problems were commonly reported as causes for negative reviewer judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of whether the proposed project can realistically be executed with the proposed resources, timeline, and personnel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to evaluate resources needed to implement the research process. One of the six most frequent criteria (present in 8 studies). Feasibility was one of the few criteria applied across applicant, project, and environment. Review notes its central role when reviewers judge budgets, timelines, and deliverability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation of the applicant's drive, commitment, and stated reasons for undertaking the proposed research (often considered a psychological attribute).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used exclusively to assess the applicant and appears rarely (reported only in Lamont 2009 among the included studies). Treated in the review as part of a 'psychological' perspective on applicant assessment; inclusion of such criteria can raise fairness concerns if applied inconsistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Traits
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment of personal characteristics or personality-related attributes of the applicant (e.g., leadership, perseverance) as relevant to their capacity to carry out the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also used only for applicant assessment and very rare (reported only in Lamont 2009). The review groups traits with motivation under a psychological perspective and flags that such person-focused criteria are conceptually different from project-focused quality criteria and can introduce bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consideration of sociological attributes such as demographic diversity or diversity of perspectives/teams when evaluating the applicant or team.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grouped with motivation and traits in a small community focused on person/sociological assessment. Diversity was one of the criteria that could be applied to applicant, project, and environment; its use reflects broader policy or equity goals but also raises issues about how and when it should influence merit assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: General relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad, non-specified notion of relevance (used in some studies at a general level rather than explicitly academic or extra-academic relevance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defined in the review as a more general term used by some studies; rare in frequency (with 'quality' it occurred infrequently). When present, it's often a high-level label that subsumes academic and extra-academic relevance and should be unpacked for operational clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other (residual) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Residual category for additional criteria mentioned in included studies that do not fit the 14 named criteria (covers idiosyncratic or rarely reported dimensions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors retained a residual 'other' category indicating that the 15 criteria do not exhaustively capture all possible evaluative dimensions. The review found that studies sometimes report unique or context-specific criteria; researchers or funders should document and define such extras explicitly to support transparency and content validity.
